title: Efficient MPO Construction for Long-Range Hamiltonians with Periodic Boundary Conditions: Application to Many-Body Dynamics
abstract: Matrix product operator (MPO) serves as a fundamental component in tensor network simulations of quantum many-body dynamics. We employ an MPO construction that introduces additional propagation channels to embed both periodic boundary conditions and finite-range couplings directly into an open boundary MPO. We apply this construction within the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) framework to simulate quench dynamics in a spin-1/2 chain with finite-range interactions, and benchmark the results numerically against the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method, finding excellent agreement for both single-body and two-body observables. The approach offers a practical route for tensor network simulations of many-body dynamics in periodic finite-range systems.
summary: This paper introduces a novel and efficient Matrix Product Operator (MPO) construction designed to handle long-range interactions on quantum spin chains with periodic boundary conditions. By embedding the PBC structure directly into the MPO formalism, the authors enable accurate time evolution simulations using the TDVP framework. The method is validated against high-accuracy classical benchmarks, offering a practical tool for studying complex many-body dynamics on rings.
main_problem: Developing an efficient Matrix Product Operator (MPO) construction to simulate quantum many-body dynamics in systems with long-range interactions under Periodic Boundary Conditions (PBC).
main_result: The proposed systematic MPO construction accurately simulates quench dynamics in spin-1/2 chains under PBC, showing excellent agreement with the RK4 benchmark method.
method: The authors generalize the MPO formalism by embedding PBC and finite-range couplings directly into an open boundary MPO structure, utilizing the Time-Dependent Variational Principle (TDVP) for time evolution.
model_or_system: The study focuses on a spin-1/2 chain governed by a Hamiltonian containing both nearest-neighbor and finite-range interactions. The simulation is performed on lattices with both open and periodic boundary conditions.
key_observables: Single-body and two-body observables, and spatial correlation functions.
important_parameters: Interaction range ($r$), system size ($N$), and the bond dimension ($D$), which grows quadratically for PBC ($D_{	ext{ring}}^r \propto r^2$).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that the PBC structure can be efficiently incorporated into the MPO framework without destroying the canonical gauge or causing excessive bond dimension inflation, which is a known issue with standard trace-based methods.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates interaction patterns for OBC and PBC. Figure 3 compares the computational runtime scaling with interaction range ($r$) and system size ($N$) for both boundary conditions.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops the MPO construction for finite-range interactions, first addressing the OBC case, then extending it to PBC by adding independent propagation channels. Finally, it validates the method by benchmarking against RK4 and analyzing the computational scaling.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial algorithmic advancement for simulating complex, realistic quantum systems (like those with long-range interactions) on periodic lattices, overcoming known limitations of standard tensor network techniques.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic illustration of ﬁnite-range interactions and peri- odic boundary conditions used for the MPO construction. (a) The 1D chain with OBC, where interactions of diﬀerent ranges are repre- sented by diﬀerent line styles. (b) The corresponding periodic chain forms a ring, highlighting the additional interaction terms introduced by the PBC. These interaction patterns determine the additional prop- agation channels required in the MPO representation.

FIG. 2. Numerical benchmark of TDVP against RK4 method for quantum dynamical evolution. (a) Time dependence of the average occupation number n. (b) Relative error of the occupation number. (c) Time evolution of the absolute values of three spatial correlation functions Cr(r = 1, 2, 3) displayed on a base-10 logarithmic vertical axis. (d) Relative errors of the correlation functions versus evolution time. The gray dashed lines indicate the transitions between diﬀerent stages of the quench protocol.

FIG. 3. Computational cost of the TDVP simulations as a function of the interaction range and system size. OBC and PBC results are represented by brown ﬁlled squares and orange ﬁlled circles, respec- tively. (a) Runtime as a function of the maximum interaction range r for N = 24, with second-order polynomial ﬁts shown as solid lines. The inset shows the OBC runtime as a function of the corresponding MPO bond dimension DOBC r , where green diamonds and a green solid line denote the data and second-order polynomial ﬁt, respec- tively. (b) Runtime as a function of system size N for r = 3, with linear ﬁts shown as solid lines.
